drills.q: A teammate says 'just use JSON mode.' What exactly does JSON mode guarantee and not guarantee?
drills.a: It guarantees syntactically valid JSON — that's all. No required keys, no value types, no enums, no key-set restriction: the model can emit {} or a misspelled key in perfect JSON. Prompting-only schema following was measured under 40% on gpt-4-0613. The fix for shape is Structured Outputs/constrained decoding or a repair loop, not JSON mode.

drills.q: You get a 200 response from a strict structured-output call but the text violates your schema. What are the two documented causes and how do you detect each?
drills.a: (1) Safety refusal — the refusal path bypasses the grammar by design: OpenAI returns a refusal field, Anthropic stop_reason 'refusal'; you were billed. (2) Truncation — max_tokens cut mid-generation: finish_reason 'length' (OpenAI) / stop_reason 'max_tokens' (Anthropic), output structurally incomplete. Detection: read the finish/stop reason fields BEFORE parsing; never discover truncation via a JSON parse error, because the fix (token budget, continuation) differs from a model misbehavior fix.

drills.q: Your extraction schema uses minimum: 0 and maxLength: 40 on fields. On Anthropic the request fails; via the Python SDK on another provider it succeeds but the constraints are never enforced. Explain both behaviors.
drills.a: Anthropic documents numeric ranges (minimum/maximum/multipleOf) and string lengths (minLength/maxLength) as outside the supported subset — unsupported keywords produce a 400 at request time, the honest failure. The SDK path silently transforms the schema: it strips unsupported keywords and appends them to field descriptions, so the constraint becomes a suggestion the model may ignore. Both mean the grammar cannot enforce those constraints — you need code validation plus the repair loop.

drills.q: Derive why an FSM-based constrained decoding engine cannot handle a recursive schema, and name OpenAI's canonical example.
drills.a: A recursive schema like a UI component tree (children: {items: {$ref: '#'}}) nests to arbitrary depth; matching brackets at arbitrary depth requires counting, which needs a stack — a pushdown automaton. An FSM has finitely many states and no memory, so it cannot distinguish nesting levels and either rejects the schema or caps depth. This is why OpenAI compiled JSON Schema to a CFG, not an FSM/regex. Note: Anthropic's subset does not support recursive schemas at all, so recursion is a per-provider capability question.

drills.q: You enable strict mode. Validity goes to 100%. Accuracy drops 6 points on your eval. What happened and what are the fixes, in order of effectiveness?
drills.a: The format tax: format restrictions measurably degrade reasoning, stricter formats worse; JSON is the worst common offender. Most of the loss is in the format-REQUESTING instructions in the prompt, not the decoder mask. Fixes: (1) free-text reasoning field inside the schema (constrained envelope, unconstrained thought); (2) two-pass — freeform generation then a cheap reformat call under the strict schema; (3) re-run the constrained-vs-unconstrained A/B per model — recent closed-weight models measured near tax-free, open-weight models still pay.

drills.q: Explain why constrained decoding overhead gets WORSE at high batch size, when GPU costs amortize.
drills.a: The model forward pass batches and amortizes on the GPU. The grammar engine does not: per-step automaton advancement and mask computation run per-sequence on the CPU, and sequences with different schemas/states don't vectorize. More batch = more GPU throughput = the CPU side becomes the bottleneck. Measured extreme: at batch 256 over 10,000-value choice sets, vLLM+XGrammar hit 7.5 req/s versus 219 req/s with precomputed trie masks — a 29x cardinality-wall gap. That asymmetry is why engine optimizations (context-independent precompute, vocab-independent stack classification) are all CPU-side.

drills.q: Design the retry policy for a structured extraction endpoint. Why is the cap 3, and what must each retry attempt contain that a naive implementation omits?
drills.a: Cap 3 (instructor's default): each retry is a full inference pass, and if the model hasn't fixed a NAMED, SPECIFIC error in 3 attempts it's a schema/prompt problem, not sampling luck — unbounded retries are a cost bomb (a model update that drops first-shot validity turns every request into 3-5 passes). Each retry must feed back the pydantic ValidationError as loc + msg (field path and the corrective action) and CHANGE something — identical re-ask at low temperature reproduces the same failure (same-error thrash). After the cap: field-level salvage of the last raw output, nulls, needs_review flag, human queue — never a 500 to the caller.

drills.q: Your product accepts customer-uploaded JSON Schemas for extraction. A security review asks what the risk is. What do you tell them, with numbers?
drills.a: Schemas are an input channel to the grammar compiler — the Constrained Decoding Attack class (CCS 2026). EnumAttack hides payloads in enum values; DictAttack decouples payload across a benign prompt and a dictionary-based grammar: 94.3-99.5% attack success rate on flagship models (gpt-5, gemini-2.5-pro, deepseek-r1, gpt-oss-120b), and still 75.8% against SOTA jailbreak guardrails — the grammar ENFORCES the payload into the output while the model completes the harmful intent, and internal safety alignment can't see the control plane. Mitigations: audit untrusted schemas like SQL — allowlist keywords, cap enum cardinality and pattern complexity, cap compile time (also a DoS vector: 10-60s compiles).

drills.q: A provider updates their model snapshot and 8% of your structured calls start failing. Walk through the response and the prevention as a postmortem.
drills.a: Response: alert on first-attempt-validity delta from per-schema instrumentation (not user complaints); pin the previous snapshot immediately; triage failures into classes (fence-wrapping, field-dropping, enum-case drift, refusal-rate change — each has a different fix); fix the highest-frequency class in prompt/schema; canary the new model with validity as the rollback trigger, not CPU/5xx — a structured-output regression is invisible to infra metrics. Prevention: treat the schema as a versioned contract with a golden conformance suite run against candidate models BEFORE cutover (like contract-testing a new downstream service); avoid undocumented behaviors (implied field presence, informal ordering). Pinning is the incident response, not the posture — deprecation timelines end.

drills.q: Should chain-of-thought live inside the structured output? Give the decision framework, not a yes/no.
drills.a: Usually yes, as a free-text field — it's the standard format-tax mitigation (constrained envelope, unconstrained thought). Three caveats: (1) register effect — merely requesting JSON narrows which answers the model produces (modal share 41%->64%), so generate diversity-critical ideation unconstrained and structure it in a second pass; (2) cost — JSON-embedded CoT pays escaping/structure overhead on every reasoning token, so two-pass (freeform then reformat) is often cheaper; (3) security — a reasoning field is untrusted model-generated text your system stores or feeds to tools; treat it as injection surface. Routing: extraction tasks -> single-pass constrained, no CoT needed; quality-critical human-facing -> two-pass; latency-critical -> single-pass constrained and eat the measured tax on the few reasoning-heavy cases.
